meta.title: Who Carries the Cherry Seed
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses direct address.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 150w at FK 4.9, part_2 108w at FK 5.2, part_3 130w at FK 6.8. The load is direct address, rhetorical questions, and playful word choice such as 'winged or legged'.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Henry David Thoreau, "The Succession of Forest Trees" (1860), in Excursions, under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Thoreau, Henry David. "The Succession of Forest Trees." 1860. In Excursions. Project Gutenberg eBook #9846, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9846, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Split long sentences, replaced rare words, dropped local asides; no facts added.
source.survey: A naturalist explains how birds carry cherry seeds into new ground.
source.avoided: No invented species, places, or counts.

session.difficulty_basis: direct address, rhetorical questions, and playful word choice such as 'winged or legged'

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Every one of these seeds, too, will be found to be winged or legged in another fashion. It is not strange that cherry trees of all kinds spread widely, since many birds like their fruit. Eating cherries is a bird-like job; if we do not drop the seeds now and then, as birds do, I shall think the birds have the best right to them. See how cleverly a cherry seed is placed so a bird must carry it. It sits right in the middle of a tempting fruit. So the creature that would eat it must usually take the stone into its mouth or bill. So these seeds have no plant wings. But Nature has made thrushes take them into their bills and fly away with them. They are winged in another sense. And they are carried better than pine seeds, which are carried even against the wind.
passage.part_2: They are cut down. A year or two later, you see oaks and other hard woods come up there; there is hardly a pine among them. But the seed has not lain in the ground so long. Each year, many four-legged animals and birds plant it. Near here, oaks and pines are spread about equally. If you look through the thickest pine wood—even one that seems all pitch pine—you will often find many little oaks, birches, and other hard woods. They come from seeds carried into the thicket by squirrels and other animals, and blown there too; but the pines shade them and choke them.
passage.part_3: The thicker the evergreen wood, the more likely it is to be well planted with these seeds, because planters tend to bring their food to the nearest cover. This planting goes on every year, and the oldest seedlings die every year. But when the pines are cleared off, the oaks have just the start they want and good conditions, so they spring up at once into trees. But when you cut off a lot of hard wood, the little pines mixed with it often get a similar start, because squirrels carry the nuts to the pines, not to the more open wood. They commonly make pretty clean work of it. If the wood was old, the sprouts will be weak or fail. The soil is somewhat used up for this crop.

items.prompt: The writer says cherry seeds are 'winged in another sense.' What carries them away?

tutor_only.confirm: Thrushes or birds carry the seeds in their bills.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'But Nature has made thrushes take them into their bills and fly away with them' states that thrushes carry the seeds.
tutor_only.tell: Cherry seeds lack plant wings. Thrushes carry them in their bills instead.
help: Look at the sentence that begins 'But Nature has made...'
Notice who takes the seed into its bill.
tutor_only.core_idea: Cherry seeds have no plant wings; thrushes carry them in their bills.
accept_ideas: Thrushes carry cherry seeds in their bills.
Birds fly away with the seeds.
Birds carry the seeds instead of plant wings.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the wind carries cherry seeds.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence names the creature that carries the seeds?

tutor_only.full_idea: Cherry seeds have no plant wings; thrushes carry them in their bills.

items.prompt: Which sentence says that thrushes carry the seeds, after saying the seeds have no wings?

tutor_only.confirm: The sentence 'But Nature has made thrushes take them into their bills and fly away with them.'
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'But Nature has made thrushes take them into their bills and fly away with them' links the birds' eating to carrying the seed.
tutor_only.tell: Cherry seeds lack plant wings. Thrushes carry them in their bills and fly away.
help: Read the sentence that begins 'But Nature has made thrushes...' and note what the birds do.
Connect the stone in the fruit to the thrush's bill and flight.
tutor_only.core_idea: The author playfully calls cherry seeds winged because thrushes carry them in their bills and fly away.
accept_ideas: Thrushes take cherry seeds in their bills and fly away.
Birds carry the seeds in their mouths or bills when they fly off.
The seeds are 'winged' because birds carry them.
not_required: Using the exact phrase 'winged in another sense'
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say cherry seeds have plant wings.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says these seeds have no plant wings?

if_they_say.when: They say birds eat the fruit and leave the seed on the tree.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence tells where the thrush takes the stone?

tutor_only.full_idea: The author playfully calls cherry seeds winged because thrushes carry them in their bills and fly away.

items.prompt: What conclusion about thick pine woods does the author support with the little oaks?

tutor_only.confirm: Pines shade and choke little oaks, so thick pine woods may hold oak seeds without many tall oaks.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence "but the pines shade them and choke them" supports the conclusion that little oaks do not grow well under thick pines.
tutor_only.tell: The pines shade the little oaks and choke them, so young oaks stay small under pines.
help: Read the sentence that starts "If you look through the thickest pine wood."
Think about what "choke" means for a young tree.
accept_ideas: Little oaks do not grow well under pine shade.
A pine wood can have many oak seeds but few tall oaks.
Pines keep young oaks from thriving.
not_required: explaining what happens after pines are cut
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say squirrels choke the little oaks.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says what shades and chokes the little oaks?

tutor_only.full_idea: Pines can shade and choke young oaks, so a thick pine wood may have many oak seeds but few growing oaks.

items.prompt: Earlier the author says birds carry cherry seeds. Why does he write 'four-legged animals' here instead of 'animals'?

tutor_only.confirm: It sets the walking carriers against the flying ones, so both kinds are named.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part one says thrushes carry cherry seeds in their bills and fly away; part two's 'four-legged animals and birds' names the carriers that walk as well, so the phrase marks a second kind of carrier.
tutor_only.tell: Birds carry cherry seeds in their bills, so 'four-legged' marks the carriers that walk instead.
help: Look at the sentence 'Each year, many four-legged animals and birds plant it.'
Compare the carriers that walk with the birds that fly.
tutor_only.core_idea: It contrasts animals that walk with the birds that fly.
accept_ideas: It contrasts animals that walk with the birds that fly.
Mammals carry the seeds on foot, not birds.
Squirrels and other walking animals carry seeds, not only birds.
The carriers walk instead of flying, so 'four-legged' says which kind.
not_required: The exact number of legs on each animal
Explaining how wind carries pine seeds
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the phrase means only birds plant seeds.
if_they_say.ask: Which word in the sentence names animals with four legs?
Which noun does 'four-legged' describe in that sentence?

partial.when: The student says the phrase makes the animals look small, or names small animals without saying they walk rather than fly.
partial.ask: What does 'four-legged' add next to the birds the author described earlier?

tutor_only.full_idea: It sets the animals that walk against the birds that fly, so both kinds of carrier are named.

items.prompt: The opening asks you to picture a bird carrying a cherry seed. What does the last part do instead?

tutor_only.confirm: It explains a cause and its result: the pines are cut, so the oaks grow.
tutor_only.correct_reason: 'See how cleverly a cherry seed is placed so a bird must carry it' invites a picture. 'But when the pines are cleared off, the oaks have just the start they want... so they spring up at once into trees' explains a cause and its result.
tutor_only.tell: The opening shows you a bird. The last part explains why the oaks grow.
help: Reread the opening and find where the author asks you to see a bird with a cherry seed.
Reread the last part and find a sentence with 'when' and 'so' that tells a result.
tutor_only.core_idea: It explains a cause — the pines are cut, so the oaks grow.
accept_ideas: it explains a cause — the pines are cut, so the oaks grow
it tells why the oaks come up after the pines are cleared
it explains what happens when the pines are cut so the oaks grow
not_required: Explaining the whole squirrel planting process
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.
